https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/20/nort.text: North Korea on Sunday carried out a launch of a "suspected ballistic missile," the Japanese Prime Minister's office said, while South Korea's military reported that Pyongyang had fired an "unidentified projectile" into the East Sea.It comes after North Korea this week rejected a resolution by the UN nuclear watchdog against its nuclear programme.A spokesperson for the country's Foreign Ministry said the International Atomic Energy Agency's resolution had "no effect on the DPRK's position as a nuclear weapons state."In August, Trump told reporters that North Korean leader Kim Jong-un had "57 very powerful nuclear weapons" as he once again touted the pair's relationship."You know what, the fact that I get along with him, that's a good thing not a bad thing," Trump said, adding that Pyongyang's nuclear arsenal should "never" have been allowed to happen.Trump announced at the time that he also intended to meet with Kim later this year, although he gave no further details on the plan - which would be their first meeting since Trump's first term in the White House.On Friday, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said he was "urging" Trump to maintain dialogue with Pyongyang, adding that Seoul was working to facilitate talks between the North and the US."I cannot say for certain how likely it is, but it is also clear that we must make every possible effort to turn that possibility into reality," he said of the potential for a meeting between US and North Korean officials.However, hopes for an imminent meeting may have been doused slightly after Kim's powerful sister, Kim Yo Jong, criticised recent military drills in the Western Pacific, which she labelled a "US-led war rehearsal."The US, South Korea and Japan wrapped up Exercise Freedom Edge 26, which US Pacific Command said advanced "trilateral readiness across the Indo-Pacific," on 11 September."Our will to defend our sovereignty will be expressed in clearer action and there will be never ever change in the course of intensifying the nuclear war deterrence," Kim Yo Jong added in a statement shared by North Korea's KCNA state news agency on Friday.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: A destroyed car outside a burned home the day after Israeli settlers reportedly attacked people and property in Jalud in the occupied West Bank. Photograph: Erik Marmor/Getty Images View image in fullscreen A destroyed car outside a burned home the day after Israeli settlers reportedly attacked people and property in Jalud in the occupied West Bank. Photograph: Erik Marmor/Getty Images US Senate US Senate blocks resolution demanding accountability over Israeli violence in West Bank Nine American citizens have been killed by Israeli settlers or security forces in occupied West Bank since 2022 Joseph Gedeon in Washington Tue 29 Sep 2026 20.16 EDT Last modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 21.41 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The US Senate on Tuesday evening rejected along mostly party lines a Democratic resolution that would have forced the state department to report to Congress on violence in the occupied West Bank , including the killings of nine American citizens by Israeli settlers or security forces over the last few years. The resolution, led by the Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen, would have given the state department 30 days to report to Congress on those deaths and on wider human rights conditions in the territory, including Israel’s detention of Palestinian children. The resolution failed to advance by a vote of 47 to 51. Pennsylvania senator John Fetterman, a Democrat, joined Republicans in voting against the resolution, while Kentucky Republican Rand Paul voted in favor. Van Hollen was able to force the vote under section 502B of the Foreign Assistance Act, a law that lets senators demand human rights reports on countries receiving US military aid. The measure drew 24 Democratic sponsors, including Bernie Sanders of Vermont, Tim Kaine of Virginia and Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the foreign relations committee. “While I was pleased that so many of my Democratic colleagues joined this effort, it’s clear the United States must do more,” Van Hollen said in a statement after the vote. “It is our responsibility to ensure recipients of US taxpayer dollars act in line with our laws and our values – this resolution was an opportunity to shed light on a reality that flies in the face of that principle.” Nine Americans have been killed in the occupied West Bank since 2022. The most recent include Sayfollah Musallet, a 20-year-old from Tampa, Florida, who was beaten to death by Israeli settlers in July 2025 while visiting family in the village of Sinjil. His family said the settlers surrounded him for more than three hours and blocked an ambulance from reaching him as he tried to protect their land. Weeks later, Khamis Ayyad, a 40-year-old father of five from Cicero, Illinois, died of smoke inhalation after settlers set fire to cars and homes in the village of Silwad. Two other Americans, both 17, Tawfic Abdel Jabbar and Mohammad Khdour, were shot dead in separate incidents in early 2024. Ayşenur Ezgi Eygi, a 26-year-old raised in Seattle, was shot in the head by Israeli troops, and Amer Rabee, a 14-year-old from New Jersey, was shot 11 times, according to Van Hollen. The victim list also includes the journalist Shireen Abu Akleh , killed in 2022, and Omar Assad, an elderly man who died after Israeli soldiers bound and gagged him. Van Hollen said none of the cases has ended in accountability, from either the Israeli or US government, and he places the blame largely on Republican senators who continue to vote against it. “If the killing of nine Americans does not justify a report from our own state department, I would ask my colleagues: what would?” the Maryland Democrat said in a floor speech. “How many more Americans must be killed before the executive branch does its job? These families deserve answers.” In August, 45 Democratic senators signed a letter to Benjamin Netanyahu urging him to act to protect Americans in the West Bank. The vote comes amid what human rights groups describe as rising settler violence. Human Rights Watch in August reported that settler attacks, together with a rapid expansion of settlements, had fully or partly displaced 107 Palestinian communities, about 5,900 people, since January 2023. The group cited UN figures showing more Palestinians were displaced in the first four months of 2026 than in all of 2025. A UN report from March covering the 12 months up to October 2025 documented 1,732 settler attacks causing injuries or property damage, and determined that Israel’s settlement expansion had forced more than 36,000 Palestinians from their homes. Many of the Democrats , who have historically been in lockstep with Israel, have now shifted over the last few years. When Sanders first forced a Senate vote on blocking arms sales to Israel in November 2024, 18 senators backed him. Then, in April of this year, 40 of the 47 Democrats voted to block a $295m sale of bulldozers to Israel, which Sanders argued would be used to demolish homes in the West Bank, Gaza and Lebanon. Another 36 voted to block a $152m sale of 1,000lb bombs. The measures failed because every Republican voted against them. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3kg.text: Figure caption, How a harrowing trial of two murdered Australian surfers ended in a guilty verdict By Will Grant ,Â BBC's Mexico Correspondent Â and Â Joel Guinto Published 6 hours ago A Mexican judge has sentenced three men convicted of murdering Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson and their US friend Carter Rhoad to 158 years and nine months in jail each. The Robinsons and Rhoad were killed in an apparent botched robbery of their truck on a secluded beach in Baja California in 2024 while they were on a surfing trip, the court heard during the trial. The murders sent shockwaves around the world, particularly in Australia, as the area is usually safe from the violence seen in other parts of Mexico. The guilty verdict was handed down last week. Debra Robinson, the brothers' mother, told the courtroom that her sons' murders had taken "the future we had imagined with them". The convicted killers' full names were not given for legal reasons, meaning they were only identified as JesÃºs Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Ãngel JesÃºs. In November last year, the girlfriend of the alleged ringleader, JesÃºs Gerardo (alias "El Kekas"), was sentenced in a separate trial to 20 years in prison. She had admitted to involvement in the robbery. The court heard that the bodies of the victims were found dumped down a well with gunshot wounds to their heads. At the time, the murders shocked locals and tourists in the beach town of Ensenada who were disturbed at the apparent ease and sheer pointlessness of the killings. Ensenada has a reputation as a welcoming spot for surfers, but the chilling murders revealed how commonplace such extreme violence remains in Mexico. The only explanation the authorities were able to give was that the surfers - all in their early 30s - had ultimately been murdered for being in the wrong place at the wrong time. Their killings happened barely 36 hours after they crossed into Mexico from the US. Their bodies, however, were not found for another week, when their families were able to identify them. Local surfers also called for greater security for residents and visiting tourists, citing other recent examples of violence in the state. Tourism is a key part of the regional economy in Baja California. https://www.politico.eu/article/parliame.text: BRUSSELS — The center-right European People's Party joined forces with far-right lawmakers Thursday to push through a vote delaying a key EU climate law governing the methane emissions of oil and gas companies. It was the latest example of the European Parliament's biggest group ignoring old taboos and working with the far right to pass legislation weakening environmental rules. The EU Methane Regulation requires fossil fuel companies to monitor and report emissions of methane, a potent greenhouse gas that's a major cause of global warming. Advertisement Advertisement The requirements were due to come into force in 2027, but the Commission last week proposed delaying implementation by a year following intense lobbying from the oil and gas lobby and the U.S. government. The EPP proposed going further, calling for a three-year delay. The amendment passed by 326 votes to 244, with the support of far-right groups Patriots for Europe, the group of Marine Le Pen's National Rally; and Europe of Sovereign Nations, the group of the German far-right party the AfD. Giorgia Meloni's European Conservatives and Reformists also backed the proposal. Most lawmakers from other centrist and center-left groups, including Renew Europe, Socialists and Democrats and the Greens, opposed the three-year delay. The right-wing majority also voted for an amendment that would force the Commission to review the law and propose any necessary changes by mid-2029. It comes a year after the EPP — the group of Commission President Ursula von der Leyen — set a new precedent when it sided with the far right to vote to weaken environmental reporting rules for companies, breaching the so-called cordon sanitaire . Since 2024, right wing groups have made up a majority in Parliament. Thursday's vote, if adopted by other EU institutions, would move the deadline for implementation of rules to 2030 — well beyond the Commission’s proposed delay to 2028. Advertisement Advertisement It comes after a months-long pressure campaign by oil and gas companies, which claimed that key elements of the rules requiring them to monitor and track leaks of the potent greenhouse gas were unclear, risking compliance failures that could deter critical supplies from reaching Europe. The Parliament's position aligns it with industry's own call for a three-year delay, and lawmakers echoed the sector's concerns about the risk of supply disruptions linked to hasty implementation of the rules. "The postponement of the requirements for oil and gas importers in the Methane Regulation is a matter of political responsibility ... We need legally certain rules in place ... to safeguard Europe’s energy supply and competitiveness," MEPs Andrea Wechlser and Christian Ehler, both in the EPP, said in a statement to POLITICO. "The crisis in the Middle East is already putting massive pressure on energy markets—about 20 percent of global LNG trade passes through the Strait of Hormuz," they added. The Parliament's position could empower national delegations — which failed to agree on a joint position Wednesday after pushback from Germany, Italy and Poland — pushing for a longer delay. Member countries hope to find a compromise next Wednesday after failing to find agreement earlier this week. CORRECTION: This article has been updated to reflect that Parliament voted to delay the rules until 2030. Advertisement Advertisement
